n: Jotham became king at twenty-five and reigned sixteen years (about 750–735 BC, partly as regent for his leprous father). His mother Jerushah was a daughter of Zadok, perhaps from the priestly family.
Jotham did right like his father — but, unlike Uzziah, he did not intrude into the temple. Sadly, the people still acted corruptly; a good king could not force good hearts.

f.w: he entered not into the temple of the LORD
f.g: He did not repeat Uzziah’s sin of usurping the priests’ role.

n: He built the Upper Gate of the temple and did extensive work on the wall of Ophel, the hill between the temple and the City of David.

f.g: The fortified ridge just south of the temple mount.

n: He built towns in Judah’s hill country and forts and towers in the wooded areas to protect the land.
Jotham defeated the Ammonites, who paid him heavy tribute — 100 talents of silver and 10,000 measures each of wheat and barley — for three years.

f.g: Hebrew kor — a large dry measure, about 6 bushels.

n: Jotham became strong because he ordered his life before the Lord his God. Steady, deliberate faithfulness brings strength.

f.w: he prepared his ways before the LORD
f.g: He established or directed his conduct according to God’s will.

n: His wars and other deeds were recorded in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
The Chronicler repeats his age and length of reign, perhaps to close his story neatly.
Jotham died and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz, one of Judah’s worst kings, succeeded him.
